name: Lolak

new_statements.quote: 2.1 Stress Similar to the other Mongondow-Gorontalo languages, stress is not contrastive in Lolak, in contrast to most of the core Central Philippine languages such as Tagalog, Cebuano, and Bikol. As can be observed in the audio files included throughout this paper, stress in Lolak regularly falls on the word-final syllable, even in Indonesian loanwords where it would be expected to fall on the penultimate syllable instead.[10] [fn. 10:] Note that this stress pattern in Lolak is observable not only in words pronounced in isolation as in the recordings accompanying this paper, but also in regular speech, including in the recordings of spontaneous discourse mentioned in footnote 8.
new_statements.citation: Lobel & Paputungan 2017 supporting audio (c. 1000 wav/mp3 word and sentence recordings), ScholarSpace hdl:10125/24758
new_statements.locator: §2.1 'Stress', p. 334 (PDF page 7), with footnote 10 on the same page

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record (our earlier survey-2026-08-31) codes Lolak as penultimate (final stress); Lobel & Paputungan state that stress regularly falls on the word-FINAL syllable and is non-contrastive. Same language (Lolak of Bolaang Mongondow), different placement: final, not penult.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is non-contrastive and falls regularly on the last syllable of the word; this holds even for Indonesian loanwords, which keep their final stress rather than the penultimate stress they would have in Indonesian, and it holds in connected speech as well as in citation forms (the authors point to the accompanying audio as the evidence).
new_statements.exceptions: None stated; the authors explicitly say the pattern extends to Indonesian loanwords (no loanword exception) and to spontaneous discourse.
new_statements.identity_note: Lobel & Paputungan describe the Lolak language of Lolak village and neighbouring settlements in Bolaang Mongondow regency, North Sulawesi (Mongondow-Gorontalo subgroup, Greater Central Philippine); the article is a field-notes sketch based on the authors' own elicitation from the last fluent speakers, with the audio bundled in the same ScholarSpace item. No dialect split is described.

readall_conflicts: The only listed work, Lobel & Paputungan 2017 (§2.1, p. 334), states unambiguously that Lolak stress is non-contrastive and falls regularly on the word-final syllable, even in Indonesian loanwords, and the authors point to the accompanying audio recordings as the evidence. This directly contradicts the catalog's our earlier survey-2026-08-31 record, which codes Lolak as penultimate. the catalog record has no quote attached, so the penult coding looks like an unsupported default (perhaps carried over from Indonesian or from a generic Philippine-type assumption) rather than a described pattern. Recommend re-coding Lolak to final stress on the authority of Lobel & Paputungan 2017.

audit.reasoning: Coding 'fixed-dominant, final (final stress)' rests on an explicit stress section in the best available description (Lobel & Paputungan 2017, specialist fieldwork sketch with audio), now downloaded and verified verbatim at p. 334. The only other descriptive work (Danie et al. 1996, 425 pp) was downloaded via the Internet Archive and is silent on stress, so nothing contradicts the classification.
